title: the day the whole people says sorry together
hook: the day the whole people says sorry together

segments.voice: Yesterday: minyan, the count of ten. Your line was some things need company. Today, a day when the room fills up. Day eighteen.

It's the tenth day of the seventh month, just after sunset, and the synagogue is full, with faces that don't come every week. Some are dressed in white. Some are wearing sneakers under their good clothes. The fast began before sunset, and it won't end until the stars come out tomorrow night. Then a cantor begins a melody so old and so familiar that some people cry before a word is sung, and it's sung three times, each time a little louder. From this evening to the next, a whole people will say sorry, together. Today: Yom Kippur.
screen: `A FULL ROOM AT SUNSET.` → `WHITE CLOTHES, NO FOOD.` → `A MELODY SUNG THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Yom Kippur means the day of atonement. The Torah sets it on the tenth day of the seventh month, in the autumn, and tells the people to afflict their souls, which the rabbis understood as a fast. So from evening to evening: no food, no water, no leather shoes, no washing for pleasure. White clothes are common, like angels, some say, who don't need to eat. The evening begins with Kol Nidre, the melody from the start, whose Aramaic words release vows. And then the confessions. They're in the plural. Not I have sinned. We have. One confession runs through the Hebrew alphabet, a wrong for every letter, and everyone says every line, lightly tapping their chest, including lines about things they personally never did. The whole community stands together as one. Nobody is singled out, and nobody gets to pretend they're above it. But the day has a limit, and the rabbis wrote it down plainly. Yom Kippur atones for what's between a person and God. For what's between you and another person, it doesn't, until you've made it right with them. So in the days before, the custom is to call, write, knock on doors, and ask forgiveness. The fast doesn't replace the phone call. In the afternoon, the story of Jonah is read: a whole city that turns around and is given another chance. As the sun goes down, the last service is called Neilah, the closing of the gates. The doors of the ark stay open, the room stands, and at nightfall one long blast of the ram's horn ends it. Then everybody goes home and eats.
screen: `THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` · `WE HAVE SINNED, NOT I.` · `THE FAST DOESN'T REPLACE THE CALL.` · `NEILAH — THE CLOSING OF THE GATES.` · then, large: `ONE LONG BLAST OF THE SHOFAR.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Bring to mind one person you owe an apology, big or small, recent or old. Don't write the speech yet. Just picture their face, and picture the moment of saying it. Notice what makes it hard. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to make the call.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement: a day of fasting, confessing together, and closing gates. Eighteenth word.
Your line: you can start over. A whole people says so, out loud, every year. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Yom Kippur Jews fast from sunset to nightfall the next day, wear no leather shoes, often dress in white, and spend much of the day in synagogue, from Kol Nidre in the evening to Neilah and the final shofar blast at nightfall; in the days before, it's customary to ask forgiveness of people one has wronged.

original.note: Hebrew: the day of atonement. the Torah calls it yom ha-kippurim.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Jewish day of fasting.
what it means: a whole people confessing together in the plural, and a limit: wrongs against people need those people.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 16 and 23 set the tenth of the seventh month; Mishnah Yoma 8:9 draws the line between sins against God and against another person.
